title: Vital Signs
summary: Every number you will take on a patient, how to take it correctly, what it means mechanically, and when it lies. Includes the age ranges, the brain scores, and the trends that matter more than any single reading.

lessons.title: Pulse: rate, rhythm, quality
lessons.body:
## What you are actually feeling

Each time the left ventricle contracts it ejects blood into an aorta that is already full. That creates a pressure wave which travels down the arterial tree faster than the blood itself. Where an artery runs over bone near the surface, you can feel that wave. That is a pulse.

Two things follow. A pulse means the heart is generating enough pressure to produce a wave, and the strength of the wave tells you something about stroke volume.

> **Key:** A pulse is a mechanical event, not an electrical one. A monitor showing an organized rhythm with no pulse is pulseless electrical activity, and that patient is in cardiac arrest.

## Three things to report, never one

1. **Rate** — beats per minute
2. **Rhythm** — regular or irregular
3. **Quality** — strong, weak, thready, or bounding

Quality is the one beginners skip and the one that carries perfusion information. Weak and thready means a small stroke volume. Bounding means a large, forceful one.

## Where to feel, and when

| Site | Where | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| Radial | thumb side of the wrist | Default in any conscious adult or child |
| Carotid | side of the neck | Unresponsive adult or child; the last pulse to disappear |
| Brachial | inner upper arm | Infants under `1` year; also the blood pressure listening site |
| Femoral | groin crease | Central pulse when the carotid is not available |
| Dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial | top of foot, behind the ankle bone | Checking circulation past a leg injury or splint |

Two rules for the carotid. Check one side at a time, never both, because compressing both can cut blood flow to the brain. And press gently, because heavy pressure there can trigger a vagal response and slow the heart.

In an infant under one year, use the **brachial** pulse. A short neck with baby fat makes the carotid unreliable and easy to compress.

## Central versus peripheral

Peripheral pulses fade first as perfusion falls. Central pulses persist longer. So a sick adult with a palpable carotid but no radial pulse has told you something: peripheral perfusion is already failing.

Older teaching assigned exact systolic pressures to each site, such as a radial pulse meaning a systolic of at least `80`. That mapping is not reliable enough to treat as fact, but the direction is real. You lose pulses from the outside in.

## Counting

| Interval | Multiply by | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `15` seconds | `4` | Regular pulse, stable patient, need speed |
| `30` seconds | `2` | The usual compromise |
| `60` seconds | `1` | Irregular rhythm, infant, or any unstable patient |

A `15`-second count carries up to four beats per minute of error from rounding alone, and an irregular rhythm makes it far worse. Count a full minute whenever the rhythm is irregular.

## Fast and slow, and why

**Tachycardia** in an adult is over `100`. Causes: pain, fear, fever, exertion, blood or fluid loss, low oxygen, stimulants, thyroid excess, and every family of shock.

**Bradycardia** is under `60`. Causes: a trained athlete at rest, sleep, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers, vagal stimulation, hypothermia, rising pressure inside the skull, heart block, and late hypoxia.

> **Trap:** In a child, bradycardia is hypoxia until proven otherwise. A child's heart slows when it runs out of oxygen, and that is a pre-arrest finding, not a calm one.

> **On shift:** Take the radial pulse while you are still introducing yourself. Rate, rhythm, quality, skin temperature and skin moisture all arrive in one touch, before the patient has said a word.
keyPoints: Report rate, rhythm and quality, not just a number.
Radial for conscious adults, carotid for unresponsive adults, brachial for infants under 1 year.
Peripheral pulses fade before central ones, so carotid-only is a perfusion finding.
Count a full 60 seconds whenever the rhythm is irregular or the patient is unstable.
Adult tachycardia is over 100 and bradycardia under 60; pediatric bradycardia means hypoxia until proven otherwise.

checks.q: You are assessing an unresponsive 6-month-old. Which pulse site is correct?
choices: Carotid
Brachial
Radial
Dorsalis pedis
checks.why: An infant's short, soft neck makes the carotid hard to find and easy to compress, so the brachial pulse in the inner upper arm is the standard site under 1 year. Radial and pedal pulses are peripheral and unreliable in a poorly perfused infant.

checks.q: A patient's pulse feels irregular. How long should you count?
choices: 15 seconds and multiply by 4
20 seconds and multiply by 3
A full 60 seconds
30 seconds and multiply by 2
checks.why: Short counts assume beats are evenly spaced, and an irregular rhythm breaks that assumption, so a 15-second sample can be off by a wide margin. A full minute is the only accurate option with an irregular pulse.

checks.q: A 4-year-old in respiratory distress now has a heart rate of 52. What does this most likely mean?
choices: The child is calming down and improving
The child is a well-conditioned athlete
The child received a beta blocker
The child is hypoxic and close to arrest
checks.why: Children compensate for low oxygen with tachycardia, so a slowing heart means the compensation has failed and arrest is near. Interpreting pediatric bradycardia as calming is a classic and lethal error.

lessons.title: Respirations: rate, depth, effort, sound
lessons.body:
## Four observations, and rate is the weakest

Breathing is assessed on four axes. Beginners report only the first.

1. **Rate** — breaths per minute. Adult normal `12`–`20`.
2. **Depth** — the tidal volume, seen as chest rise. Roughly `500 mL` per breath in an adult, of which about `150 mL` never leaves the airway tubing and never reaches the alveoli.
3. **Effort** — how much work it costs the patient.
4. **Sound** — what you hear with and without a stethoscope.

A rate of `20` with shallow breaths and a straining neck is far worse than a rate of `24` with easy, full breaths.

> **Key:** Rate alone never tells you whether breathing is adequate. Rate times depth is the amount of air actually reaching gas exchange.

## Counting without the patient knowing

People change their breathing the moment they know you are watching it. The standard workaround: finish taking the radial pulse, keep your fingers on the wrist and your eyes on the chest, and count respirations during the next interval. The patient still thinks you are counting the pulse.

Count `30` seconds and double it for a regular pattern. Count a full `60` seconds if the pattern is irregular, if the patient is an infant, or if the patient is unstable. Infants normally breathe irregularly with short pauses, which is one more reason for a full minute.

## Work of breathing

These signs say the patient is spending energy to breathe, and they appear before the numbers go bad.

- **Accessory muscle use** — neck and shoulder muscles pulling with each breath
- **Retractions** — skin sucking in between the ribs, above the collarbones, or below the sternum. The single most useful pediatric sign.
- **Nasal flaring** — nostrils widening, mostly in infants and small children
- **Tripod position** — sitting forward on braced arms to give the chest room
- **Head bobbing** — an infant's head nodding with each breath
- **Grunting** — an infant exhaling against a partly closed throat to hold alveoli open. Always significant.
- **Speaking in short phrases or single words** — a fast, free severity scale
- **One-word dyspnea** — cannot complete a sentence. This is severe.

## Sounds

| Sound | Where | Usually means |
|---|---|---|
| Snoring | upper airway, no stethoscope needed | Tongue partly blocking the airway |
| Gurgling | upper airway | Fluid: vomit, blood or secretions. Suction. |
| Stridor | high-pitched, heard on inhaling | Narrowing at the larynx: croup, swelling, foreign body |
| Wheezing | whistling, mostly on exhaling | Narrowed lower airways: asthma, COPD, anaphylaxis |
| Crackles (rales) | fine popping, on inhaling | Fluid in alveoli: heart failure, pneumonia |
| Absent or diminished | one side or both | Pneumothorax, severe asthma, poor air movement |

> **Trap:** A silent chest in an asthmatic is not improvement. Wheezing requires air movement to produce sound, so a wheeze that disappears while the patient looks worse means almost no air is moving. That is an emergency.

## Abnormal patterns

**Agonal breathing** is slow, irregular, gasping. It looks like breathing and it is not. It is a brainstem reflex in the first minutes of cardiac arrest, and mistaking it for respirations is the most common reason CPR gets delayed. An unresponsive adult with no pulse and gasping breaths is in arrest. Start compressions.

**Kussmaul** respirations are deep, fast and sighing, blowing off carbon dioxide to compensate for metabolic acid, classically in diabetic ketoacidosis.

**Cheyne-Stokes** breathing cycles between deeper and shallower breaths with pauses in between, and it is seen in severe brain injury and end-stage illness.

> **On shift:** Count how many words a breathless patient can say in one breath and write it down. Full sentences, short phrases, or single words. Repeat it in ten minutes and you have a trend anyone can interpret.
keyPoints: Assess rate, depth, effort and sound; adult normal is 12–20 breaths per minute.
Count respirations while pretending to still take the pulse, because awareness changes the pattern.
Work of breathing signs: retractions, accessory muscle use, nasal flaring, tripod position, grunting.
A silent chest in an asthmatic means almost no air is moving, not improvement.
Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest, not breathing; start compressions.

checks.q: Why do you count respirations while keeping your fingers on the patient's wrist?
choices: It keeps the pulse count accurate at the same time
Patients change their breathing pattern when they know it is being watched
It is required for documentation
It warms the patient's hand and improves circulation
checks.why: Breathing is partly under voluntary control, so awareness of being observed changes rate and depth. Leaving your hand on the wrist lets the patient believe you are still counting the pulse.

checks.q: An asthmatic who was wheezing loudly is now quiet, sleepy and working hard to breathe. What does this mean?
choices: The bronchodilator is working and the attack is resolving
The patient is simply tired and needs rest
Air movement has dropped so low that no wheeze can be produced; this is critical
The stethoscope is positioned incorrectly
checks.why: Wheezing is turbulent air moving through narrowed tubes, so it requires airflow to exist. Losing the wheeze while the patient deteriorates means airflow has nearly stopped, which is impending respiratory arrest.

checks.q: An unresponsive adult has no pulse and is taking occasional slow gasping breaths. What is the correct action?
choices: Give oxygen by non-rebreather and monitor the breathing
Place the patient in the recovery position
Withhold CPR because the patient is breathing
Begin chest compressions immediately
checks.why: Agonal gasps are a brainstem reflex during early cardiac arrest and provide no effective ventilation. Treating them as breathing is the most common cause of delayed CPR, and every minute of delay lowers survival substantially.

lessons.title: Blood pressure: what it is and how to measure it
lessons.body:
## The two numbers, physically

**Systolic** is the peak pressure in the arteries at the instant the left ventricle contracts. It reflects how forcefully the heart ejects.

**Diastolic** is the pressure remaining between beats, while the ventricle refills. It reflects how tightly the arterioles are squeezed, because that resistance is what keeps pressure from falling to zero between beats.

So the top number is mostly about the pump, and the bottom number is mostly about the pipes. That is why a patient clamping down hard in early shock shows a rising diastolic before the systolic ever moves.

EMS vital-sign references list roughly `90`–`140` systolic over `60`–`90` diastolic as the acceptable adult range. Diagnostically, the 2017 ACC/AHA classification is tighter: normal is under `120/80`, elevated is `120`–`129` systolic with diastolic under `80`, stage 1 hypertension starts at `130/80`, and stage 2 at `140/90`. Hypotension in an adult is often quoted as a systolic under `90`.

> **Key:** Blood pressure is cardiac output multiplied by vessel resistance. A normal reading can hide a failing pump if the vessels are squeezing hard enough to cover it.

## Manual auscultation, step by step

1. Patient seated or supine, arm supported at the level of the heart. An arm hanging low reads falsely high; an arm held above the heart reads falsely low.
2. Place the cuff on the bare upper arm, lower edge about `1` inch (`2.5 cm`) above the elbow crease, with the bladder centered over the brachial artery.
3. Find the radial pulse and inflate until it disappears. Note that number. This is your estimate.
4. Deflate fully, wait about `30` seconds, then place the stethoscope diaphragm over the brachial artery in the elbow crease.
5. Reinflate to about `20`–`30 mmHg` above your estimate.
6. Deflate slowly, `2`–`3 mmHg` per second. Faster than that and you will read low on the systolic and high on the diastolic.
7. The first clear tapping sound is the **systolic**. The point where sound disappears is the **diastolic**.

## Korotkoff sounds

Those tapping noises have a name. When the cuff squeezes the artery to a partial closure, blood squirting through the narrowed opening becomes turbulent and audible.

| Phase | Sound | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| I | First clear tapping | Systolic pressure |
| II | Softer swishing | |
| III | Crisper, louder tapping | |
| IV | Abrupt muffling | Diastolic in children and pregnancy, by some conventions |
| V | Silence | Diastolic in adults |

When no cuff pressure is applied, flow is smooth and silent. Fully occluded, there is no flow and no sound. Sound exists only in between, which is exactly why the two ends of the sound define the two numbers.

## Palpated systolic

When noise makes listening impossible, or the patient is critical and you need a number now, palpate instead. Inflate until the radial pulse disappears, then deflate slowly and note where it returns. Chart it as, for example, `90/P` for palpated.

A palpated reading gives you a systolic only, and it typically reads a few millimeters lower than an auscultated one. You cannot get a diastolic by palpation.

## Cuff size, the error nobody checks

The inflatable bladder inside the cuff should be about **`40%`** of the arm's circumference in width and about **`80%`** of it in length.

- A cuff that is **too small** must be squeezed harder to compress the artery, so it reads **falsely high**. This is the common error, and it mislabels large-armed patients as hypertensive.
- A cuff that is **too large** reads **falsely low**, which can hide real hypotension in a thin or pediatric patient.

> **Trap:** Taking a pressure over clothing, with a bent arm, or on the arm that has an `IV` running, a dialysis fistula, or a mastectomy on that side, gives a bad number or harms the patient. Use the other arm.

> **On shift:** If a reading surprises you, repeat it yourself with the correct cuff in the other arm before you act on it or report it. Roughly a third of alarming pressures in a busy department are technique.
keyPoints: Systolic is peak ejection pressure (the pump); diastolic is the resting pressure between beats (the pipes).
Inflate 20–30 mmHg above the point where the radial pulse disappears, then deflate 2–3 mmHg per second.
Korotkoff phase I is the systolic and phase V, the disappearance of sound, is the adult diastolic.
Palpated systolic is charted as a number over P and gives no diastolic.
Bladder width should be 40% of arm circumference; too-small cuffs read falsely high, too-large read falsely low.

checks.q: You deflate a blood pressure cuff at about 8 mmHg per second. What is the effect?
choices: No effect; deflation speed does not change the reading
The systolic reads falsely low and the diastolic falsely high
Both numbers read falsely high
Only the diastolic is affected
checks.why: Fast deflation skips past the first Korotkoff sound before you register it and reaches silence before true diastole, compressing both numbers toward each other. The standard rate of 2–3 mmHg per second exists to prevent exactly this.

checks.q: A large-armed patient is measured with a standard adult cuff and reads 168/96. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The cuff is too small for the arm, producing a falsely high reading
The cuff is too large, producing a falsely high reading
The reading is accurate and requires immediate treatment
The stethoscope was placed over the radial artery
checks.why: A bladder narrower than 40% of arm circumference requires extra pressure to compress the artery, so the gauge overstates the true pressure. A too-large cuff produces the opposite error, reading falsely low.

checks.q: You chart a blood pressure as 88/P. What does that mean?
choices: The diastolic was 88 and the systolic could not be heard
The pressure was taken with an automatic machine
The patient was prone during measurement
The systolic was 88, obtained by palpation, with no diastolic available
checks.why: Palpation detects the return of the radial pulse during deflation, which marks systolic pressure only, since there is no palpable event corresponding to diastole. The P notation tells the next reader how the number was obtained.

lessons.title: Making blood pressure mean something: MAP, pulse pressure, orthostatics
lessons.body:
## Mean arterial pressure

Organs are not perfused by the systolic peak. They are perfused by the average pressure across the whole cardiac cycle, which is called the **mean arterial pressure** (`MAP`).

The heart spends roughly one third of each cycle in systole and two thirds in diastole, so the average is weighted toward the diastolic number.

`MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3`

Work one: a pressure of `120/80` gives `(120 + 160) / 3 = 93 mmHg`.

Work another: a pressure of `100/50` gives `(100 + 100) / 3 = 67 mmHg`. The systolic of `100` looks acceptable. The `MAP` of `67` is barely above the line.

**`MAP 65 mmHg` is the number to remember.** Below roughly that, the kidneys and brain can no longer autoregulate their own blood flow and perfusion starts falling with pressure. It is the standard resuscitation target in sepsis and shock care.

> **Key:** The diastolic gets twice the weight in the `MAP` formula because the heart spends twice as long there. That is why a falling diastolic is worse news than most beginners expect.

## Pulse pressure

Pulse pressure is simply systolic minus diastolic, normally `30`–`40 mmHg`.

**Narrow** pulse pressure, under about `25 mmHg`, means the diastolic has climbed toward the systolic. The arterioles are clamped. Think early hypovolemic shock, cardiac tamponade, or severe aortic stenosis.

**Wide** pulse pressure, over about `60 mmHg`, means the diastolic has dropped away. Think dilated vessels in distributive shock, or rising pressure inside the skull, where a widening pulse pressure with bradycardia and irregular breathing forms Cushing's triad.

A reading of `118/96` has a normal systolic and a pulse pressure of `22`. The patient is compensating hard. Reading only the top number would have missed it entirely.

## Orthostatic vital signs

Standing up drops about `500`–`800 mL` of blood into the legs. A normally hydrated person compensates in seconds. A volume-depleted person cannot, and orthostatic measurement makes that visible.

**Method:**

1. Lie the patient supine for `2`–`3` minutes, then take pulse and blood pressure.
2. Have them stand, or sit with legs dangling if standing is unsafe.
3. Wait `1` minute, then repeat pulse and blood pressure. Many protocols repeat again at `3` minutes.
4. Stay with the patient the entire time. Some of them will faint, and that is the point of the test.

**Positive if any of these:**

- Systolic falls by `20 mmHg` or more
- Diastolic falls by `10 mmHg` or more
- Heart rate rises by `20` beats per minute or more
- The patient becomes dizzy, gray, or nearly faints, regardless of the numbers

That last criterion outranks the others. Symptoms on standing are a positive test even if every number stays inside the thresholds.

> **Trap:** Do not perform orthostatics on a patient who is already hypotensive, actively bleeding, has an unstable pelvis or leg fracture, or has a suspected spinal injury. You already have your answer, and standing them up can only hurt them.

## When the automatic cuff lies

Oscillometric machines do not hear Korotkoff sounds. They measure the amplitude of pressure oscillations in the cuff, detect the peak, and then calculate the systolic and diastolic from that peak using a proprietary formula.

That design produces specific failures:

- **Irregular rhythms**, especially atrial fibrillation, confuse the oscillation analysis
- **Shivering, seizing, or moving** patients produce artifact
- **Very low pressures** compress the oscillation signal, and the machine tends to over-read a truly low pressure, which is the worst possible direction of error
- **Wrong cuff size** produces the same errors as with a manual cuff
- A machine that keeps re-inflating and finally displays a number has usually failed several attempts first

> **On shift:** Any machine reading that would change your management gets confirmed manually. In a hypotensive patient, a manual pressure is not a formality, it is the real number.
keyPoints: MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3, and MAP 65 mmHg is the perfusion floor for brain and kidneys.
Pulse pressure is SBP minus DBP, normal 30–40; narrow under 25 suggests clamped vessels and early shock.
Widening pulse pressure with bradycardia and irregular breathing is Cushing's triad from rising intracranial pressure.
Orthostatics are positive with a 20 mmHg systolic drop, a 10 mmHg diastolic drop, a 20 bpm pulse rise, or symptoms.
Automatic cuffs tend to over-read genuinely low pressures; confirm manually before acting.

checks.q: A patient's blood pressure is 100/50. What is the MAP and what does it mean?
choices: 75 mmHg, comfortably above the perfusion threshold
67 mmHg, only just above the 65 mmHg perfusion floor
50 mmHg, well below the threshold
83 mmHg, entirely normal
checks.why: MAP is (100 + 2 × 50) / 3 = 200 / 3 = 67 mmHg. The systolic of 100 looks acceptable on its own, but the low diastolic drags the mean down to the edge of where organs stop autoregulating.

checks.q: A trauma patient's pressures over 20 minutes read 124/76, then 120/88, then 118/96. What is happening?
choices: The patient is stable because the systolic has barely changed
The readings show equipment error
The pulse pressure is narrowing, indicating progressive vasoconstriction and early shock
The patient is becoming hypertensive
checks.why: Pulse pressure falls from 48 to 32 to 22 mmHg as the diastolic climbs toward the systolic, which is arteriolar clamping to defend pressure. Watching only the systolic would show a patient who looks unchanged while compensation runs out.

checks.q: Which patient should NOT have orthostatic vitals performed?
choices: A 62-year-old with a supine BP of 78/44 and ongoing rectal bleeding
A 30-year-old with two days of vomiting and a supine BP of 116/72
A 70-year-old reporting lightheadedness on standing with a supine BP of 124/70
A 45-year-old with dizziness after starting a new blood pressure medication
checks.why: A patient who is already hypotensive and actively bleeding has given you the answer, and standing them adds only risk of syncope and injury. Orthostatics are for patients whose supine numbers still look acceptable.

lessons.title: Pulse oximetry and when it lies
lessons.body:
## How it works

A pulse oximeter shines two wavelengths of light through a finger: red at about `660 nm` and infrared at about `940 nm`. Hemoglobin carrying oxygen absorbs those two wavelengths differently from hemoglobin that is empty.

The device measures how much of each wavelength arrives at the sensor on the far side, isolates the pulsing (arterial) portion of the signal, and calculates the percentage of hemoglobin that is saturated. That is `SpO2`.

Two limits are baked into that description. It measures **saturation, not oxygen content**, and it needs a **pulsatile signal** to work at all.

> **Key:** `SpO2` tells you the percentage of hemoglobin seats that are filled. It cannot tell you how many seats exist. A severely anemic patient can read `100%` and still be starved of oxygen.

## The numbers

| Reading | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `95%`–`100%` | Normal on room air |
| `94%` | The usual treatment threshold in adults |
| `91%`–`93%` | Hypoxia; investigate and treat |
| `90%` or below | Severe hypoxia; act now |
| `88%`–`92%` | The target range in many chronic `COPD` protocols |

The `94%` line is not arbitrary. The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is flat above roughly `90%` saturation and then falls off a cliff below it. A drop from `99%` to `94%` reflects a small change in dissolved oxygen. A drop from `90%` to `85%` reflects a large one. Below `90%`, small further drops in `SpO2` mean big drops in actual oxygen delivered.

## When it lies, and which direction

**Falsely high or falsely normal:**

- **Carbon monoxide poisoning.** Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light almost identically to oxyhemoglobin at `660 nm`, so the device counts it as saturated. A patient dying of `CO` can read `100%`. This is the single most dangerous false reading in the field, and it requires a `CO`-oximeter or a blood gas to detect.
- **Anemia.** All the remaining hemoglobin can be fully loaded while there is simply not enough of it.

**Falsely low or no reading:**

- **Cold fingers and poor perfusion** — the most common cause. Weak pulsatile signal means nothing to measure. Warm the hand, or move to an earlobe or the forehead.
- **Motion** — shivering, seizing, tremor, a moving vehicle
- **Dark nail polish and artificial nails** — blue, green and black interfere most. Remove it, or turn the probe sideways across the finger.
- **Severe vasoconstriction** from shock or cold exposure
- **Methemoglobinemia** pulls readings toward roughly `85%` no matter the true saturation

**Skin pigmentation bias.** Pulse oximeters were calibrated predominantly on light-skinned subjects, and multiple large studies have shown they overestimate true arterial saturation in patients with darker skin. Occult hypoxemia, meaning a true saturation below `88%` while the device shows `92%`–`96%`, occurs roughly three times more often in Black patients than in white patients. The practical response is to weight the clinical picture more heavily and to treat borderline readings as lower than displayed.

> **Trap:** A good waveform or signal-quality bar tells you the reading is real. It does not tell you the reading is correct. Carbon monoxide produces a beautiful waveform and a lethal, reassuring number.

> **On shift:** When `SpO2` disagrees with the patient, believe the patient. Someone gasping, tripoding, and speaking in single words with a reading of `97%` still has a breathing emergency.
keyPoints: Pulse oximetry measures the percentage of hemoglobin saturated, not the amount of oxygen present.
94% is the usual adult treatment threshold; many COPD protocols target 88–92%.
Carbon monoxide poisoning and anemia both produce falsely reassuring readings.
Cold fingers, poor perfusion, motion and dark nail polish produce falsely low or absent readings.
Oximeters overestimate saturation in darker-skinned patients, so treat borderline numbers as lower than shown.

checks.q: A patient rescued from a house fire is confused with a headache and reads SpO2 100% on room air. What is happening?
choices: Oxygenation is excellent and the confusion is unrelated
The probe is malfunctioning and should be replaced
Carboxyhemoglobin is being counted as saturated hemoglobin, so the reading is falsely reassuring
The patient is hyperventilating and blowing off oxygen
checks.why: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and absorbs light nearly identically to oxygen at the wavelengths used, so a standard oximeter cannot distinguish them. Detection requires a CO-oximeter or blood gas, and treatment is high-flow oxygen regardless of the displayed number.

checks.q: Why does the 94% threshold matter more than a drop from 99% to 96%?
choices: Below roughly 90% the dissociation curve steepens, so small drops in SpO2 mean large drops in delivered oxygen
Readings above 94% are always inaccurate
94% is the point at which the device switches calculation methods
The threshold is arbitrary and varies by manufacturer
checks.why: The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is flat at high saturations and falls steeply below about 90%, so the same percentage change means very different amounts of oxygen. That physiology is why treatment thresholds sit just above the shoulder of the curve.

checks.q: A hypothermic patient in shock gives no pulse oximetry reading at the fingertip. What is the best explanation?
choices: The patient has no oxygen in the blood
Peripheral vasoconstriction and cold have removed the pulsatile signal the device needs
The probe requires a blood pressure over 140 systolic
Hypothermia destroys hemoglobin
checks.why: The device isolates the pulsing arterial portion of the light signal, so clamped, cold peripheral vessels leave it nothing to measure. Warming the hand or moving to an earlobe or forehead probe often restores a reading.

lessons.title: Temperature and pain
lessons.body:
## Temperature and where you take it

Normal core body temperature averages `37.0 C` (`98.6 F`), with a normal range of roughly `36.5`–`37.5 C` (`97.7`–`99.5 F`). It runs about `0.5 C` lower in the early morning than in the late afternoon, which is a real physiologic swing rather than an error.

The route changes the number, so the route must be charted with the value.

| Route | Relative to oral | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rectal | about `0.5 C` (`1 F`) higher | Closest to true core; the standard in infants and in hypothermia |
| Oral | reference | Falsely low after cold drinks or in a mouth breather |
| Axillary | about `0.5`–`1 C` (`1 F`) lower | Least accurate; a screening value only |
| Tympanic | roughly `0.3 C` higher | Fast but very technique-dependent; wax and angle matter |
| Temporal artery | varies | Screening; skewed by sweat and ambient temperature |

> **Key:** A temperature without a route is an incomplete measurement. An axillary `37.4 C` and a rectal `37.4 C` describe two different patients.

## The thresholds

- **Fever** is a temperature of `38.0 C` (`100.4 F`) or higher. In an infant under `3` months, a rectal temperature at or above that number is an emergency evaluation, not a wait-and-see.
- **Hypothermia** is a core temperature under `35.0 C` (`95 F`). Mild is `32`–`35 C`, moderate `28`–`32 C`, severe below `28 C`.
- **Severe hyperthermia** is a core temperature over `40 C` (`104 F`).

## Fever versus hyperthermia

This distinction changes treatment, so it is worth getting exactly right.

**Fever** is the body deliberately raising its own thermostat in response to infection. The set point moves up, so the patient shivers and feels cold while running hot. Antipyretics such as acetaminophen work because they lower the set point back down.

**Hyperthermia**, as in heat stroke, is the body losing to its environment. The thermostat never moved. The patient is producing or absorbing more heat than they can shed. Antipyretics do nothing at all, because there is no raised set point to lower. The treatment is physical cooling, and in heat stroke that means aggressive cooling immediately.

Heat stroke is defined by a core temperature over `40 C` **plus altered mental status**. Hot skin with confusion after exertion or environmental exposure is a true emergency with a short window.

> **Trap:** Giving acetaminophen for heat stroke wastes the only time that matters. Fever needs the set point lowered; hyperthermia needs heat physically removed.

## Pain as a vital sign

Pain is subjective, which makes it easy to dismiss and important to measure consistently.

**Numeric scale, `0`–`10`.** Ask it the same way every time: zero is no pain, ten is the worst pain imaginable. What matters clinically is not the absolute number but the change over time and with treatment.

**Wong-Baker FACES.** Six cartoon faces, usable from about age `3`, and useful for adults with language barriers or cognitive impairment. The patient points; you do not interpret their expression.

**FLACC** is used for preverbal children and scores Face, Legs, Activity, Cry and Consolability by observation.

## PQRST, the structured history

For any pain, this framework produces a usable description in under a minute. Many services teach it as `OPQRST`, adding Onset at the front.

| Letter | Ask |
|---|---|
| **P** | Provocation and palliation: what makes it worse, what makes it better |
| **Q** | Quality: sharp, dull, crushing, burning, tearing. Use their words. |
| **R** | Region and radiation: where is it, does it travel |
| **S** | Severity: `0`–`10`, now and at its worst |
| **T** | Time: when did it start, constant or intermittent, has it changed |

The answers carry diagnostic weight. Crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw or left arm suggests cardiac. Tearing pain radiating to the back suggests aortic dissection. Pain reproducible by pressing on the chest wall is more likely musculoskeletal, although that finding never rules out a heart attack on its own.

> **On shift:** Chart the patient's own words in quotation marks for the quality. "Like an elephant on my chest" carries more information to the next clinician than "chest pain, `8/10`."
keyPoints: Normal core temperature is about 37.0 C (98.6 F); always chart the route with the value.
Fever is 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher; hypothermia is under 35 C (95 F); severe hyperthermia is over 40 C (104 F).
Fever is a raised set point and responds to antipyretics; hyperthermia is environmental and needs physical cooling.
Heat stroke is core temperature over 40 C plus altered mental status.
Use 0–10 for adults, FACES from about age 3, FLACC for preverbal children, and PQRST to structure the pain history.

checks.q: A 24-year-old collapses during a summer road race with hot dry skin, confusion and a rectal temperature of 41.2 C. What is the priority?
choices: Give acetaminophen to lower the fever
Begin aggressive physical cooling immediately
Warm blankets and oral fluids
Wait for the temperature to normalize on its own
checks.why: This is heat stroke, defined by a core temperature over 40 C with altered mental status, and the body's thermostat was never raised. Antipyretics have nothing to act on, so only removing heat physically addresses the problem.

checks.q: Why must the route be documented alongside a temperature?
choices: It determines the billing code
Different routes require different thermometers
Routes differ systematically, so the same number means different things
Only rectal temperatures are legally valid
checks.why: Rectal readings run about 0.5 C above oral and axillary readings run about 0.5 to 1 C below, so an identical displayed number can represent a febrile or an afebrile patient. Without the route, the next reader cannot interpret or compare the value.

checks.q: A patient describes chest pain that is tearing and radiates straight through to the back. Which part of PQRST captured that, and why does it matter?
choices: P and S, indicating a musculoskeletal cause
Q and R, because tearing quality with back radiation suggests aortic dissection
T alone, since only timing is diagnostic
S alone, since severity determines the diagnosis
checks.why: Quality captured the tearing character and Region and radiation captured the path to the back, which together form the classic dissection description. Severity and timing matter but do not distinguish causes the way quality and radiation do.

lessons.title: Vital signs of the brain: AVPU, GCS and glucose
lessons.body:
## Why the brain gets its own vitals

The brain is about `2%` of body weight and consumes about `20%` of the body's oxygen and glucose. It has no meaningful reserve of either. That makes mental status the most sensitive perfusion monitor you own, and it needs no equipment.

Any change in mental status is a vital sign change and gets treated like one.

> **Key:** Confusion, agitation and drowsiness are not personality. They are readings. Something is wrong with the brain's supply of oxygen, glucose, blood flow, or its chemistry.

## AVPU: the fast scale

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A** — Alert | Eyes open, interacting. Grade orientation to person, place, time and event. |
| **V** — Verbal | Responds only when spoken to |
| **P** — Painful | Responds only to a painful stimulus such as a trapezius pinch |
| **U** — Unresponsive | No response to anything |

"Alert and oriented `×4`" means person, place, time and event. Orientation is lost in that rough order, so a patient who knows who they are but not the date is `A&O ×2`.

Use `AVPU` in the primary assessment because it takes three seconds. Use the Glasgow Coma Scale when you need a number you can trend and hand off.

## Glasgow Coma Scale

Three categories. Score each independently, always take the **best** response observed, and report the components as well as the total.

**Eye opening, out of `4`**

| Score | Response |
|---|---|
| `4` | Opens eyes spontaneously |
| `3` | Opens to voice |
| `2` | Opens to pressure or pain |
| `1` | No eye opening |

**Verbal response, out of `5`**

| Score | Response |
|---|---|
| `5` | Oriented, converses normally |
| `4` | Confused conversation |
| `3` | Inappropriate words |
| `2` | Incomprehensible sounds |
| `1` | No verbal response |

**Motor response, out of `6`**

| Score | Response |
|---|---|
| `6` | Obeys commands |
| `5` | Localizes to pain, reaches toward the stimulus |
| `4` | Withdraws from pain, normal flexion |
| `3` | Abnormal flexion, arms bending inward, decorticate |
| `2` | Extension, arms straightening outward, decerebrate |
| `1` | No motor response |

Total range is `3` to `15`. It cannot be lower than `3`, because every category has a minimum of `1`.

**Worked example.** A head-injured patient opens his eyes when you call his name, tells you it is `1998` and that he is at his cousin's house, and reaches up toward your hand when you pinch his trapezius.

- Eyes open to voice: `E3`
- Confused conversation, forming sentences but wrong content: `V4`
- Reaches toward the stimulus rather than pulling away: `M5`

`GCS 12` (`E3 V4 M5`). Report it that way. A total of `12` could be built several different ways, and the components are what the next clinician needs.

**Severity bands:** `13`–`15` mild, `9`–`12` moderate, `8` or below severe. A score of `8` or below has traditionally been the threshold at which the airway is considered unprotected. In children too young to speak, a modified pediatric verbal scale is used instead.

> **Trap:** Localizing (`M5`) and withdrawing (`M4`) are constantly confused. Localizing means the hand moves toward the painful stimulus to find it. Withdrawing means the limb pulls away. Moving toward requires more brain than pulling away.

## Blood glucose

The brain runs on glucose and stores essentially none, so a fingerstick is a brain vital sign.

**Technique:** clean the finger and let the alcohol dry completely, because wet alcohol dilutes the sample and reads falsely low. Use the side of the fingertip, not the pulpy center. Wipe away the first drop and test the second. Do not squeeze hard; milking adds tissue fluid and skews the result.

**The numbers:**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Fasting `70`–`99 mg/dL` | Normal |
| Random up to about `140 mg/dL` | Normal range |
| Under `70 mg/dL` with symptoms | Hypoglycemia |
| Under `54 mg/dL` | Clinically significant hypoglycemia |
| Over `250 mg/dL` with illness | Consider diabetic ketoacidosis |
| Over `600 mg/dL` | Consider hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state |

Hypoglycemia presents with confusion, sweating, tremor, combativeness, seizure or coma, and it imitates stroke or intoxication perfectly. It reverses in minutes. Hyperglycemia builds over hours to days with thirst and frequent urination, plus Kussmaul breathing and a fruity odor in `DKA`.

> **On shift:** Every altered patient gets a glucose. Every seizure, every stroke alert, every intoxicated-appearing patient, every unexplained fall in an older adult. It costs seconds and it is the one cause you can reverse at the bedside.
keyPoints: Mental status is the most sensitive perfusion monitor available and requires no equipment.
AVPU is Alert, Verbal, Painful, Unresponsive; A&O ×4 is person, place, time and event.
GCS scores eye (4), verbal (5) and motor (6) for a total of 3–15; report components, not just the total.
GCS 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, 8 or below severe; localizing is M5 and withdrawing is M4.
Hypoglycemia is under 70 mg/dL with symptoms and mimics stroke or intoxication; check a glucose on every altered patient.

checks.q: A patient opens her eyes to voice, gives confused answers, and reaches toward your hand when you apply a painful stimulus. What is her GCS?
choices: GCS 10 (E2 V4 M4)
GCS 14 (E4 V5 M5)
GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5)
checks.why: Eye opening to voice is 3, confused conversation is 4, and localizing by reaching toward the stimulus is 5, totaling 12. Withdrawing would be M4, and inappropriate single words rather than confused sentences would be V3.

checks.q: Why should the first drop of blood be wiped away during a fingerstick glucose?
choices: It contains too many red blood cells
It may be diluted by residual alcohol or tissue fluid and read falsely
It clots faster than later drops
It is required to calibrate the meter
checks.why: Residual alcohol or interstitial fluid in the first drop dilutes the sample and shifts the reading, most often downward. Squeezing hard to force blood out adds tissue fluid and produces the same distortion.

checks.q: A 68-year-old is found slurring words with left-sided weakness. What must be checked before calling a stroke alert?
choices: An oral temperature
A blood glucose
A pain score
An orthostatic blood pressure
checks.why: Hypoglycemia reproduces focal neurologic deficits including slurred speech and one-sided weakness, and it reverses within minutes of treatment. Missing it sends a treatable patient down a stroke pathway while the brain continues to starve.

lessons.title: Normal ranges by age
lessons.body:
## Why the numbers move with age

A newborn's heart is small, so each beat ejects very little blood. The only way to produce adequate cardiac output from a tiny stroke volume is to beat fast. As the heart grows, stroke volume rises and the resting rate falls. The same logic runs through respiratory rate: small lungs, small breaths, more breaths per minute.

Blood pressure rises with age because vessels lengthen and stiffen and because the growing heart generates more force.

> **Key:** You do not memorize seven tables. You memorize one idea (smaller body, faster rates, lower pressure) plus the adult numbers, and then the pediatric values are the direction of travel from there.

## The table

| Age group | Heart rate | Respiratory rate | Systolic BP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neonate, `0`–`1` month | `100`–`180` | `30`–`60` | `60`–`90` |
| Infant, `1`–`12` months | `100`–`160` | `25`–`50` | `70`–`95` |
| Toddler, `1`–`3` years | `90`–`150` | `20`–`30` | `80`–`100` |
| Preschool, `3`–`5` years | `80`–`140` | `20`–`25` | `80`–`100` |
| School age, `6`–`12` years | `70`–`120` | `15`–`20` | `80`–`110` |
| Adolescent, `13`–`18` years | `60`–`100` | `12`–`20` | `90`–`120` |
| Adult | `60`–`100` | `12`–`20` | `90`–`140` |

Ranges vary somewhat between textbooks and protocols. Learn the shape and the adult anchors, and use your service's reference for exact cutoffs.

## The two formulas worth knowing

**Minimum acceptable systolic, ages `1` to `10`:** `70 + (2 × age in years)`.

A `3`-year-old floor is `76 mmHg`. A `7`-year-old floor is `84 mmHg`. Below that number the child is hypotensive, and in a child hypotension is a pre-arrest finding.

**Expected systolic, ages `1` to `10`:** `90 + (2 × age in years)`. This is the normal value, not the floor, and the gap between the two formulas is the child's entire reserve.

## The compensation story, restated

Children compensate extraordinarily well and then fail abruptly.

A child can raise heart rate far higher than an adult and can clamp peripheral vessels hard, so a child may lose `30%`–`40%` of blood volume with a systolic pressure that still reads normal for age. Right up until it does not.

That means the useful pediatric findings are not the blood pressure. They are:

- **Heart rate** — rising first, and sustained tachycardia without fever or fear is abnormal
- **Respiratory rate and effort** — retractions, nasal flaring, grunting
- **Skin** — color, temperature, mottling, capillary refill over `2` seconds
- **Mental status** — interactive versus limp, and whether the child recognizes a parent

> **Trap:** Pediatric hypotension is a late, near-arrest sign, not an early warning. By the time a child's systolic falls below the `70 + (2 × age)` floor, the reserve is gone.

## Older adults move the other way

Aging changes how vital signs behave, and the changes all reduce your warning time.

- Vessels stiffen, so systolic pressure and pulse pressure both rise. A systolic of `110` in a chronically hypertensive `80`-year-old may represent significant hypotension for that person.
- The heart's response to sympathetic signalling blunts with age, and medications such as beta blockers blunt it further, so the compensatory tachycardia may never appear.
- Temperature regulation weakens. Serious infection in an older adult often presents with a **normal or low** temperature and confusion rather than a fever.
- Baseline cognition varies, so establishing what normal was for this person, usually from family, is part of the assessment.

> **On shift:** For any patient at either end of life, ask what their normal is before you judge the number. A resting pulse of `95` means one thing in an athlete and another in an `88`-year-old on metoprolol.
keyPoints: Smaller bodies have faster heart and respiratory rates and lower blood pressure.
Adult normals: HR 60–100, RR 12–20, systolic 90–140.
Minimum systolic for ages 1–10 is 70 + (2 × age); expected systolic is 90 + (2 × age).
In children judge perfusion by heart rate, work of breathing, skin and mental status, not blood pressure.
Older adults may not mount a tachycardia or a fever, so serious illness can present with normal-looking vitals.

checks.q: A 2-year-old has a heart rate of 168 and a respiratory rate of 34. How should these be interpreted?
choices: Both are normal for a toddler at rest
Both are above the expected toddler ranges and require explanation
Only the respiratory rate is abnormal
Only the heart rate is abnormal
checks.why: Toddler ranges are roughly 90–150 for heart rate and 20–30 for respirations, so both values sit above normal. Fear and fever can explain them, but neither can be assumed without assessing perfusion.

checks.q: An 8-year-old trauma patient has a systolic pressure of 84. What does the formula tell you?
choices: The floor is 86, so this child is hypotensive and near arrest
The floor is 70, so this is acceptable
The floor is 100, so this is only mildly low
The formula does not apply to trauma patients
checks.why: The minimum systolic for ages 1 to 10 is 70 + (2 × 8) = 86 mmHg, so 84 is below the floor. In a child, crossing that line means compensation has already failed and arrest is close.

checks.q: An 84-year-old nursing home resident is confused with a temperature of 36.4 C and a heart rate of 78. Why is serious infection still possible?
choices: Older adults always run cooler and confusion is expected with age
The normal temperature proves infection is absent
Only the heart rate is relevant in older adults
Aging and medications blunt the fever and tachycardia responses, so confusion may be the only sign
checks.why: Thermoregulation and sympathetic responsiveness both decline with age, and beta blockers suppress the tachycardia further, so sepsis commonly presents as new confusion with unremarkable vitals. Treating normal numbers as reassurance in this population misses serious infection.

lessons.title: Trends, shock index, and documenting vitals
lessons.body:
## One set of vitals is a snapshot

A single set tells you where the patient is. Two sets tell you which way they are going, and direction is what decides the plan.

A heart rate of `104` means very little on its own. A heart rate that went `88`, then `104`, then `122` over thirty minutes means the patient is losing ground, even if every individual reading sat inside a normal-looking range.

> **Key:** Take vitals twice before you decide anything, unless the first set already demands action. The second set is where the information lives.

## How often

| Patient | Repeat interval |
|---|---|
| Unstable, or any significant intervention given | every `5` minutes |
| Stable | every `15` minutes |
| After any medication that affects vitals | before, and again after |
| After any change in position, including orthostatics | with each position |

Those intervals are standard practice; your service or department may set its own. The principle does not change: an unstable patient gets measured often enough that you catch a change while you can still act on it.

## Shock index

One number combines the pulse and the pressure and often turns abnormal before either one does on its own.

`Shock index = heart rate / systolic blood pressure`

| Value | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `0.5`–`0.7` | Normal |
| `0.7`–`0.9` | Borderline; look harder |
| Over `0.9` | Associated with significantly increased mortality and transfusion need |
| Over `1.0` | The heart rate has exceeded the systolic. Treat as shock. |

Work an example. A patient at `HR 88`, `BP 118/70` has a shock index of `0.75`, which is borderline. Thirty minutes later, `HR 116`, `BP 92/60` gives `1.26`. Neither the pulse nor the pressure crossed a dramatic line by itself, but the index nearly doubled.

In pregnancy and in children the thresholds differ, and shock index supplements clinical judgment rather than replacing it. It is most useful as a trend.

## What a complete set contains

Every documented set should carry:

1. **Time**, to the minute
2. Pulse: rate, rhythm, quality
3. Respirations: rate, depth, effort
4. Blood pressure, with the method if not standard, such as `88/P`
5. `SpO2` and whether it was on room air or on oxygen, with the flow rate
6. Temperature with the route
7. Skin: color, temperature, moisture
8. Mental status: `AVPU` or `GCS` with components
9. Pain score with the scale used
10. Blood glucose when indicated

> **Trap:** An `SpO2` charted without the oxygen delivery is an unusable number. `94%` on room air and `94%` on `15 L` by non-rebreather describe two entirely different patients, and only the time and the oxygen column separate them.

## Documenting honestly

Chart what you measured, not what you expected. If a reading looks wrong, repeat it and chart both values with both times rather than discarding the one you disliked.

If a measurement could not be obtained, write why: "unable to obtain `BP`, patient combative" or "`SpO2` unobtainable, peripheries cold." A blank is unreadable to the next clinician; a stated reason is itself clinical information.

Never chart vitals you did not personally take without attributing them, and never copy forward a previous set.

> **On shift:** The most valuable thing you produce in a shift is a clean, timed trend. Physicians make decisions on the direction of your numbers, and a column of well-spaced, honestly recorded sets is often what makes a deteriorating patient visible before anything dramatic happens.
keyPoints: A single set is a snapshot; two sets give direction, which is what changes decisions.
Repeat every 5 minutes if unstable and every 15 minutes if stable, and re-check after any intervention.
Shock index = HR / SBP; normal 0.5–0.7, and over 0.9 signals significant risk.
Every set needs a time, and every SpO2 needs the oxygen delivery recorded with it.
Chart what was measured, state why a value could not be obtained, and never copy a set forward.

checks.q: A patient's readings go from HR 88 / BP 118/70 to HR 116 / BP 92/60. What are the two shock index values?
choices: 0.75 then 1.26, nearly doubling
1.26 then 0.75, improving
0.75 then 0.92, minimal change
Shock index cannot be calculated without a respiratory rate
checks.why: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure, so 88/118 = 0.75 and 116/92 = 1.26. The index crossing 1.0 means the heart rate has exceeded the systolic, which should be treated as shock.

checks.q: Why must oxygen delivery be charted alongside every SpO2 value?
choices: It is needed for equipment inventory
94% on room air and 94% on 15 L by non-rebreather describe completely different patients
The oximeter calculates differently on oxygen
It is required only in the intensive care unit
checks.why: The same saturation achieved with no support versus maximum support represents very different degrees of illness and very different trajectories. Without the delivery recorded, the number cannot be compared to the previous or next set.

checks.q: You obtain a blood pressure that seems implausibly low for the patient in front of you. What is the correct action?
choices: Discard it and chart the next reading only
Chart it without comment and take no further action
Chart an average of the two readings
Repeat it manually and chart both values with their times
checks.why: Repeating with a manual cuff distinguishes a technique or machine artifact from a real change, and charting both timed values preserves the trend for whoever reads the chart next. Discarding or averaging destroys information and can hide a genuine deterioration.

cards.front: What three things must be reported about a pulse?
cards.back: Rate (beats per minute), rhythm (regular or irregular), and quality (strong, weak, thready, bounding). Quality carries the perfusion information beginners skip.

cards.front: Which pulse site do you use for an infant under 1 year, and why?
cards.back: Brachial, in the inner upper arm. A short neck with baby fat makes the carotid hard to locate and easy to compress.

cards.front: What are the two rules for checking a carotid pulse?
cards.back: One side at a time, never both, because compressing both cuts cerebral blood flow. And press gently, since heavy pressure can trigger a vagal response and slow the heart.

cards.front: When must you count a pulse for a full 60 seconds?
cards.back: Whenever the rhythm is irregular, the patient is an infant, or the patient is unstable. Short counts assume evenly spaced beats.

cards.front: Define adult tachycardia and bradycardia, and name three causes of each.
cards.back: Tachycardia over 100: pain, fever, hypovolemia, hypoxia, stimulants. Bradycardia under 60: beta blockers, vagal stimulation, hypothermia, heart block, athletic conditioning.

cards.front: What does bradycardia mean in a child?
cards.back: Hypoxia until proven otherwise. A child's heart slows when oxygen runs out, which makes it a pre-arrest finding rather than a calm one.

cards.front: What are the four things you assess about breathing?
cards.back: Rate, depth (tidal volume seen as chest rise), effort (work of breathing), and sound. Rate alone is the least informative of the four.

cards.front: How do you count respirations accurately?
cards.back: Keep your fingers on the wrist after taking the pulse and watch the chest, so the patient believes you are still counting the pulse. Awareness changes the breathing pattern.

cards.front: Name six signs of increased work of breathing.
cards.back: Accessory muscle use, retractions, nasal flaring, tripod positioning, head bobbing in infants, grunting, and speaking in short phrases or single words.

cards.front: What does stridor indicate and where does it come from?
cards.back: A high-pitched sound on inhaling, from narrowing at the larynx or above. Causes include croup, swelling from allergic reaction, and a foreign body.

cards.front: Why is a silent chest in an asthmatic an emergency?
cards.back: Wheezing requires airflow to make sound. Losing the wheeze while the patient worsens means air movement has nearly stopped, which is impending respiratory arrest.

cards.front: What is agonal breathing and what does it require you to do?
cards.back: Slow, irregular gasping that is a brainstem reflex in early cardiac arrest, not effective breathing. An unresponsive, pulseless patient who is gasping needs chest compressions now.

cards.front: Distinguish crackles, wheezing and gurgling.
cards.back: Crackles are fine popping on inhaling from fluid in alveoli. Wheezing is whistling mostly on exhaling from narrowed lower airways. Gurgling is upper airway fluid and calls for suction.

cards.front: What do systolic and diastolic pressure physically represent?
cards.back: Systolic is peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction, reflecting the pump. Diastolic is the pressure remaining between beats, reflecting arteriolar resistance, the pipes.

cards.front: How high do you inflate a blood pressure cuff, and how fast do you deflate?
cards.back: Inflate 20 to 30 mmHg above the point where the radial pulse disappears. Deflate 2 to 3 mmHg per second; faster reads the systolic low and the diastolic high.

cards.front: Which Korotkoff phases give the systolic and the adult diastolic?
cards.back: Phase I, the first clear tapping, is the systolic. Phase V, the disappearance of sound, is the adult diastolic. Phase IV muffling is used in children and pregnancy by some conventions.

cards.front: What is a palpated blood pressure and how is it charted?
cards.back: Inflate until the radial pulse disappears, deflate slowly, note where it returns. That is systolic only, charted as a number over P, for example 90/P. No diastolic is obtainable.

cards.front: State the cuff sizing rule and both error directions.
cards.back: Bladder width about 40 percent of arm circumference, length about 80 percent. Too small reads falsely high; too large reads falsely low.

cards.front: What is the MAP formula and why is diastolic weighted double?
cards.back: MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3. The heart spends roughly two thirds of each cycle in diastole, so the average is weighted toward the diastolic pressure.

cards.front: Why does MAP 65 matter?
cards.back: Below roughly 65 mmHg the brain and kidneys can no longer autoregulate blood flow, so perfusion falls with pressure. It is the standard resuscitation target in shock and sepsis.

cards.front: What is pulse pressure, what is normal, and what does narrowing mean?
cards.back: Systolic minus diastolic, normally 30 to 40 mmHg. Narrow, under about 25, means arterioles are clamped: early hypovolemia, tamponade or aortic stenosis.

cards.front: What does a widening pulse pressure suggest, and what is Cushing's triad?
cards.back: Dilated vessels or rising intracranial pressure. Cushing's triad is widening pulse pressure with hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing, indicating brain herniation risk.

cards.front: Describe the method for orthostatic vital signs.
cards.back: Supine 2 to 3 minutes, take pulse and BP. Stand the patient, wait 1 minute, repeat; many protocols repeat at 3 minutes. Stay with them throughout.

cards.front: What makes orthostatic vitals positive?
cards.back: Systolic falls 20 mmHg or more, diastolic falls 10 mmHg or more, heart rate rises 20 bpm or more, or the patient becomes symptomatic. Symptoms count regardless of the numbers.

cards.front: When should orthostatic vitals NOT be done?
cards.back: Already hypotensive, actively bleeding, unstable pelvis or leg fracture, or suspected spinal injury. You already have the answer and standing them adds only risk.

cards.front: Why do automatic cuffs fail, and in which direction at low pressures?
cards.back: They measure oscillation amplitude, not sound, so irregular rhythms and motion confuse them. At genuinely low pressures they tend to over-read, which is the most dangerous direction.

cards.front: How does a pulse oximeter work?
cards.back: It shines red (about 660 nm) and infrared (about 940 nm) light through tissue, compares absorption, isolates the pulsing arterial signal, and calculates the percentage of hemoglobin saturated.

cards.front: Why is 94% the usual adult threshold?
cards.back: The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is flat above about 90 percent and steepens sharply below it, so small further drops in SpO2 mean large drops in delivered oxygen.

cards.front: Which two conditions make pulse oximetry falsely reassuring?
cards.back: Carbon monoxide poisoning, because carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light like oxyhemoglobin and can read 100 percent, and anemia, because the few cells present can be fully saturated.

cards.front: Name five causes of a falsely low or absent pulse oximetry reading.
cards.back: Cold fingers, poor perfusion or shock, motion or shivering, dark nail polish and artificial nails, and severe vasoconstriction. Methemoglobinemia pins readings near 85 percent.

cards.front: What is the skin pigmentation problem with pulse oximetry?
cards.back: Devices were calibrated mostly on light skin and overestimate true saturation in darker skin. Occult hypoxemia is roughly three times more common in Black patients, so treat borderline readings as lower than displayed.

cards.front: What is normal core temperature, and what are the fever and hypothermia thresholds?
cards.back: Normal averages 37.0 C (98.6 F), range about 36.5 to 37.5 C. Fever is 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher. Hypothermia is under 35.0 C (95 F).

cards.front: How do temperature routes compare to oral?
cards.back: Rectal runs about 0.5 C (1 F) higher and is closest to core. Axillary runs about 0.5 to 1 C lower and is a screening value only. Tympanic runs slightly higher and is technique-dependent.

cards.front: What is the difference between fever and hyperthermia, and why does it change treatment?
cards.back: Fever is a raised set point from infection and responds to antipyretics. Hyperthermia is environmental heat overwhelming the body with a normal set point, so only physical cooling works.

cards.front: How is heat stroke defined?
cards.back: Core temperature over 40 C (104 F) plus altered mental status. It is a true emergency requiring immediate aggressive cooling, not antipyretics.

cards.front: What fever threshold makes an infant under 3 months an emergency?
cards.back: A rectal temperature of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher. In that age group it triggers an immediate evaluation rather than watchful waiting.

cards.front: Which pain scales are used at which ages?
cards.back: Numeric 0 to 10 for adults and older children. Wong-Baker FACES from about age 3, also useful across language barriers. FLACC by observation for preverbal children.

cards.front: What does PQRST stand for?
cards.back: Provocation and palliation, Quality, Region and radiation, Severity 0 to 10, Time. Many services teach OPQRST, adding Onset at the front.

cards.front: What does AVPU stand for and what is A&O ×4?
cards.back: Alert, Verbal, Painful, Unresponsive. Alert and oriented ×4 means oriented to person, place, time and event, which are lost in roughly that order.

cards.front: Give the GCS eye-opening scale.
cards.back: 4 spontaneous, 3 to voice, 2 to pressure or pain, 1 none. Always score the best response observed.

cards.front: Give the GCS verbal scale.
cards.back: 5 oriented, 4 confused conversation, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none.

cards.front: Give the GCS motor scale.
cards.back: 6 obeys commands, 5 localizes to pain, 4 withdraws (normal flexion), 3 abnormal flexion (decorticate), 2 extension (decerebrate), 1 none.

cards.front: Score this: eyes open to voice, confused answers, reaches toward a painful stimulus.
cards.back: E3 V4 M5 = GCS 12. Report the components, since several combinations produce the same total.

cards.front: What is the GCS range, and what are the severity bands?
cards.back: 3 to 15, since each category has a minimum of 1. Mild 13 to 15, moderate 9 to 12, severe 8 or below. Eight or below has traditionally marked an unprotected airway.

cards.front: How do you tell localizing from withdrawing on the GCS?
cards.back: Localizing (M5) means the hand moves toward the painful stimulus to find it. Withdrawing (M4) means the limb pulls away. Moving toward requires more brain than pulling away.

cards.front: Describe correct fingerstick glucose technique.
cards.back: Clean and dry the finger completely, since wet alcohol dilutes the sample. Use the side of the fingertip, wipe away the first drop, test the second, and do not squeeze hard.

cards.front: Give the key blood glucose numbers.
cards.back: Fasting normal 70 to 99 mg/dL, random up to about 140. Hypoglycemia is under 70 with symptoms, clinically significant under 54. DKA is often over 250.

cards.front: Which patients must get a blood glucose check?
cards.back: Every altered mental status, seizure, suspected stroke, apparently intoxicated patient, and unexplained fall in an older adult. Hypoglycemia mimics all of them and reverses in minutes.

cards.front: Give normal adult heart rate, respiratory rate and systolic pressure.
cards.back: Heart rate 60 to 100, respiratory rate 12 to 20, systolic 90 to 140. These are the anchors from which the pediatric ranges depart.

cards.front: Why are infant heart and respiratory rates so much faster than an adult's?
cards.back: A small heart ejects a small stroke volume, so adequate cardiac output requires more beats per minute. Small lungs mean small tidal volumes and more breaths per minute.

cards.front: Give the heart and respiratory rate ranges for a neonate and for an infant.
cards.back: Neonate 0 to 1 month: HR 100 to 180, RR 30 to 60, systolic 60 to 90. Infant 1 to 12 months: HR 100 to 160, RR 25 to 50, systolic 70 to 95.

cards.front: Give the ranges for a toddler and a school-age child.
cards.back: Toddler 1 to 3 years: HR 90 to 150, RR 20 to 30, systolic 80 to 100. School age 6 to 12 years: HR 70 to 120, RR 15 to 20, systolic 80 to 110.

cards.front: State both pediatric systolic formulas for ages 1 to 10.
cards.back: Minimum acceptable systolic is 70 + (2 × age in years). Expected systolic is 90 + (2 × age). The gap between them is the child's reserve.

cards.front: In a child, which findings do you judge perfusion by instead of blood pressure?
cards.back: Heart rate, respiratory rate and effort, skin color and temperature with capillary refill over 2 seconds, and mental status. Pediatric hypotension is a near-arrest finding.

cards.front: Why can an older adult with serious infection have normal vital signs?
cards.back: Aging blunts thermoregulation and the sympathetic response, and beta blockers blunt it further. Sepsis may present as new confusion with no fever and no tachycardia.

cards.front: What is the shock index formula and what are the thresholds?
cards.back: Heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. Normal 0.5 to 0.7, borderline 0.7 to 0.9, over 0.9 signals increased mortality and transfusion need, over 1.0 treat as shock.

cards.front: How often do you repeat vital signs?
cards.back: Every 5 minutes for an unstable patient or after any significant intervention, every 15 minutes for a stable patient, and before and after any medication affecting vitals.

cards.front: Why is a single set of vital signs so limited?
cards.back: It gives position but not direction. A heart rate of 104 means little alone; 88 then 104 then 122 over thirty minutes shows a patient losing ground.

cards.front: What must be charted with every SpO2 value?
cards.back: The oxygen delivery and flow rate, or that it was room air. 94 percent on room air and 94 percent on 15 L by non-rebreather describe two different patients.

cards.front: What do you do when a vital sign cannot be obtained?
cards.back: Document why, for example unable to obtain BP because the patient is combative. A blank is unreadable; a stated reason is itself clinical information.

quiz.q: You are assessing an unresponsive 7-month-old. Which pulse site should you use?
choices: Brachial
Carotid
Radial
Posterior tibial
quiz.why: An infant's short, soft neck makes the carotid difficult to locate and easy to compress, so the brachial artery in the inner upper arm is standard under 1 year. Radial and pedal pulses are peripheral and unreliable in a poorly perfused infant.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old with severe respiratory distress develops a heart rate of 54. What does this indicate?
choices: The child is calming and improving
A normal vagal response to crying
Hypoxia with imminent cardiac arrest
An expected effect of albuterol
quiz.why: Children compensate for hypoxia with tachycardia, so a falling rate means the compensation has failed. Albuterol raises rather than lowers heart rate, which makes this finding even more alarming in a treated asthmatic.

quiz.q: A patient has an irregular pulse. How should it be counted?
choices: 15 seconds multiplied by 4
A full 60 seconds
30 seconds multiplied by 2
10 seconds multiplied by 6
quiz.why: Short counts assume beats are evenly spaced, and irregularity breaks that assumption, so a 15-second sample can be off substantially. A full minute is the only reliable option with an irregular rhythm.

quiz.q: An asthmatic patient who was wheezing loudly on arrival is now quiet, drowsy, and using accessory muscles. What has happened?
choices: The treatment has worked and the patient is resting
The stethoscope is being placed incorrectly
The patient has developed a pneumothorax on both sides
Air movement has fallen so low that no wheeze can be generated
quiz.why: A wheeze is turbulent airflow through narrowed airways and requires movement of air to exist, so losing it while the patient deteriorates means airflow has nearly stopped. Drowsiness in this context reflects rising carbon dioxide and signals impending respiratory arrest.

quiz.q: Why do you keep your fingers on the patient's wrist while counting respirations?
choices: To confirm the pulse is still present
To keep the arm warm for a later blood pressure
Because patients change their breathing when they know it is being watched
Because the pulse and respiratory rates must be counted simultaneously
quiz.why: Breathing is partly voluntary, so awareness of observation alters rate and depth. Keeping your hand on the wrist lets the patient believe the pulse count is continuing, which preserves the natural pattern.

quiz.q: An unresponsive adult has no palpable carotid pulse and is taking occasional slow gasping breaths. What is the correct action?
choices: Begin chest compressions immediately
Apply oxygen by non-rebreather and reassess in one minute
Place the patient in the recovery position
Assist ventilations only, since the patient is breathing
quiz.why: Agonal gasps are a brainstem reflex in early cardiac arrest and provide no effective gas exchange, so a pulseless patient who is gasping is in arrest. Mistaking agonal respirations for breathing is the most common cause of delayed CPR.

quiz.q: Which finding is the single most useful sign of increased work of breathing in a small child?
choices: A respiratory rate above 20
A pulse oximetry reading of 95%
A heart rate above 100
Retractions between the ribs and above the clavicles
quiz.why: Retractions show that the child is generating large negative pressures to move air, and they appear before saturation or mental status change. A respiratory rate above 20 is normal for most children, and a saturation of 95% is reassuring in isolation.

quiz.q: You deflate the blood pressure cuff rapidly, at roughly 10 mmHg per second. What error results?
choices: Both numbers read falsely high
The systolic reads falsely low and the diastolic falsely high
Only the systolic is affected
No error results as long as sounds are heard
quiz.why: Rapid deflation moves past the first Korotkoff sound before you register it and reaches silence prematurely, compressing both values toward the middle. The standard 2 to 3 mmHg per second rate exists specifically to avoid this.

quiz.q: A patient with a very large upper arm is measured with a standard adult cuff and reads 172/98. What is the most likely issue?
choices: The cuff is too large and reads falsely high
The reading is accurate and needs no confirmation
The cuff is too small for the arm, producing a falsely high reading
The stethoscope was placed over the radial artery
quiz.why: A bladder narrower than about 40 percent of arm circumference needs extra pressure to compress the artery, so the gauge overstates the true value. A cuff that is too large produces the opposite error and reads falsely low.

quiz.q: In a noisy ambulance you obtain a blood pressure by palpation. How should it be charted and what does it include?
choices: As a systolic over P, for example 92/P, with no diastolic available
As a full reading with an estimated diastolic
As a diastolic only, since palpation detects the end of flow
As an automatic reading once the machine agrees
quiz.why: Palpation detects the return of the radial pulse during deflation, which corresponds only to systolic pressure, since nothing palpable marks diastole. The P notation tells the next reader how the value was obtained.

quiz.q: A patient's blood pressure is 96/48. What is the mean arterial pressure and what does it mean?
choices: 72 mmHg, comfortably normal
48 mmHg, critically low
84 mmHg, entirely normal
64 mmHg, just below the 65 mmHg perfusion floor
quiz.why: MAP is (96 + 2 × 48) / 3 = 192 / 3 = 64 mmHg. The systolic near 100 looks survivable on its own, but the low diastolic drags the mean below the level at which the brain and kidneys can autoregulate flow.

quiz.q: A trauma patient's pressures progress from 126/74 to 122/90 to 118/98. What is the significance?
choices: The patient is developing hypertension
The pulse pressure is narrowing, indicating vasoconstriction and compensated shock
The readings are stable because the systolic has barely changed
The cuff is too small and is over-reading the diastolic
quiz.why: Pulse pressure falls from 52 to 32 to 20 mmHg as the diastolic climbs toward the systolic, which reflects arterioles clamping to defend pressure. Watching only the systolic shows an apparently stable patient while compensation is being exhausted.

quiz.q: A patient's supine vitals are HR 78, BP 124/76. After one minute standing, HR 102, BP 106/68. Are the orthostatics positive?
choices: Yes, the heart rate rose 24 beats per minute, which exceeds the 20 bpm threshold
No, because the systolic fell only 18 mmHg
No, because the diastolic fell only 8 mmHg
Cannot be determined without a three-minute reading
quiz.why: Any single criterion makes the test positive, and a rise of 20 beats per minute or more qualifies on its own. The systolic drop of 18 and diastolic drop of 8 fall short individually, which is exactly why the heart rate criterion exists.

quiz.q: Which patient should NOT have orthostatic vital signs taken?
choices: A 28-year-old with two days of vomiting and a supine BP of 118/74
A 55-year-old dizzy after starting a new antihypertensive
A 66-year-old with a supine BP of 76/42 and active rectal bleeding
A 72-year-old reporting lightheadedness on standing with a supine BP of 130/78
quiz.why: A patient already hypotensive and actively bleeding has given you the answer, and standing them risks syncope and injury with nothing to gain. Orthostatics are for patients whose resting numbers still appear acceptable.

quiz.q: A patient pulled from a smoky basement is confused with a headache and an SpO2 of 99% on room air. What should you conclude?
choices: Oxygenation is adequate and the confusion has another cause
The probe is defective and should be changed
The patient is hyperventilating and washing out oxygen
Carbon monoxide is likely present and the reading is falsely reassuring
quiz.why: Carboxyhemoglobin absorbs light almost identically to oxyhemoglobin at the wavelengths a standard oximeter uses, so it is counted as saturated. Detection requires CO-oximetry or a blood gas, and high-flow oxygen is given regardless of the displayed number.

quiz.q: A hypothermic patient in shock produces no pulse oximetry reading at the fingertip. What is the most likely cause?
choices: There is no oxygen remaining in the blood
Cold and vasoconstriction have eliminated the pulsatile signal the device requires
Hypothermia denatures hemoglobin
The device requires a systolic pressure above 140
quiz.why: The oximeter isolates the pulsing arterial portion of the light signal, so clamped cold peripheral vessels give it nothing to analyze. Warming the hand or switching to an earlobe or forehead sensor often restores a usable reading.

quiz.q: Why should a borderline SpO2 in a patient with dark skin be treated as lower than displayed?
choices: Darker skin blocks more infrared light and produces low readings
Melanin binds oxygen and reduces available hemoglobin
Oximeters calibrated mostly on light skin overestimate true saturation, making occult hypoxemia more common
The finding applies only to forehead sensors
quiz.why: Multiple large studies have shown devices overestimate arterial saturation in patients with darker skin, with true saturations below 88 percent hidden behind displayed values of 92 to 96 percent roughly three times more often. The correct response is to weight the clinical picture more heavily.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old collapses during a hot marathon with confusion and a rectal temperature of 41.4 C. What is the priority?
choices: Aggressive physical cooling immediately
Acetaminophen 1000 mg by mouth
Warm blankets and oral rehydration
Observation until the temperature falls on its own
quiz.why: Core temperature over 40 C with altered mental status is heat stroke, in which the thermostat was never raised and antipyretics have nothing to act on. Only removing heat physically addresses the mechanism, and the window for preventing organ damage is short.

quiz.q: Why must the route be charted with every temperature?
choices: Because only rectal readings are considered valid
Because routes differ systematically, so the same number describes different patients
Because different routes require different thermometers
Because the route determines the documentation code
quiz.why: Rectal readings run about 0.5 C above oral and axillary readings about 0.5 to 1 C below, so an identical displayed value can represent a febrile or afebrile patient. Without the route the next reader cannot compare the value to any other.

quiz.q: A patient reports chest pain that is tearing and radiates straight through to the back between the shoulder blades. Which PQRST elements carried that, and what does it suggest?
choices: Severity and time, suggesting a musculoskeletal strain
Provocation and palliation, suggesting reflux
Time alone, suggesting a stable pattern
Quality and radiation, suggesting aortic dissection
