quiz.why: Quality captured the tearing character and Region and radiation captured the path to the back, which together form the classic dissection description. Severity and timing are important but do not discriminate between causes the way quality and radiation do.

quiz.q: A patient opens her eyes to voice, answers questions in confused sentences, and reaches toward your hand during a painful stimulus. What is her GCS?
quiz.why: Eye opening to voice is 3, confused conversation is 4, and localizing by reaching toward the stimulus is 5, totaling 12. Withdrawing away from the stimulus would score M4, and single inappropriate words rather than sentences would score V3.

quiz.q: What is the lowest possible Glasgow Coma Scale score and why?
choices: 0, when there is no response at all
1, since all three categories collapse to one
3, because each of the three categories has a minimum of 1
5, which is the published floor for adults
quiz.why: Eye, verbal and motor each score at least 1 even in a completely unresponsive patient, so the minimum total is 3. A reported GCS of 0 or 1 is a scoring error, not a clinical finding.

quiz.q: A 71-year-old is found slurring words with right arm weakness. What must be checked before activating a stroke pathway?
choices: An orthostatic blood pressure
A tympanic temperature
A pain score using FACES
A fingerstick blood glucose
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia reproduces focal deficits including slurred speech and one-sided weakness and reverses within minutes of treatment. Missing it commits a treatable patient to a stroke pathway while the brain continues to starve.

quiz.q: Why is the first drop of blood wiped away during a fingerstick glucose?
choices: It contains an excess of platelets
It may be diluted by residual alcohol or tissue fluid and give a false value
It clots faster than subsequent drops
It is used to calibrate the meter
quiz.why: Alcohol that has not fully dried, or interstitial fluid from squeezing the finger, dilutes the sample and typically shifts the reading downward. Using the second drop from a dry, unsqueezed fingertip avoids both errors.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old trauma patient has a systolic pressure of 78. How should this be interpreted?
choices: Normal for age, since children run lower pressures
Mildly low but acceptable with a normal heart rate
Below the 82 mmHg floor from 70 + (2 × age), meaning decompensated shock
Not interpretable without a diastolic value
quiz.why: The minimum acceptable systolic for ages 1 to 10 is 70 + (2 × 6) = 82 mmHg, so 78 is below the floor. In a child, hypotension appears only after 30 to 40 percent volume loss, which makes it a pre-arrest finding.

quiz.q: Why do neonates have heart rates of 100 to 180 while adults sit at 60 to 100?
choices: A small heart ejects a small stroke volume, so adequate output requires more beats per minute
Newborn blood carries less oxygen per cell
Newborns have higher blood pressure requiring faster circulation
Newborn hearts have an immature electrical system that fires randomly
quiz.why: Cardiac output is stroke volume times rate, and a neonate's ventricle holds very little, so rate must compensate. The same principle explains the higher respiratory rate: small tidal volumes require more breaths per minute.

quiz.q: An 86-year-old nursing home resident is newly confused with a temperature of 36.6 C and a heart rate of 76. Why can this still be sepsis?
choices: Confusion is a normal finding at that age and can be ignored
Aging and beta blockers blunt both the fever and the tachycardia responses
Nursing home residents cannot develop fevers
Only the respiratory rate matters in geriatric infection
quiz.why: Thermoregulation and sympathetic responsiveness both decline with age, and rate-controlling medications suppress the tachycardia further, so infection often presents as new confusion with unremarkable numbers. Treating normal vitals as reassurance in this population misses serious illness.

quiz.q: A patient's readings move from HR 84 / BP 120/70 to HR 118 / BP 96/62 over 25 minutes. What do the shock index values show?
choices: 0.70 then 0.81, a minimal change
1.23 then 0.70, an improvement
Shock index cannot be calculated without a MAP
0.70 then 1.23, crossing the threshold into shock
quiz.why: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure, so 84/120 = 0.70 and 118/96 = 1.23. Crossing 1.0 means the heart rate now exceeds the systolic, which should be treated as shock even though neither individual value is dramatic.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 74F, dizzy when she stands up
scenarios.intro:
Dispatch: `74`-year-old female, dizziness, not a fall, patient is awake and talking. No other information.

You arrive at a tidy apartment. She is sitting in an armchair and apologizes for calling. She says she has felt fine sitting down all morning, but the room spins every time she gets up. Her daughter made her call.

Medications on the counter: lisinopril, furosemide, and a low-dose aspirin.

steps.prompt:
She is alert and oriented `×4`. Skin is slightly pale and cool, dry. Lungs clear. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, no headache, no weakness on one side.

Seated vitals are below. What do you do next?

choices.text: Lay her supine for a few minutes, then repeat vitals standing to check for orthostatic change.
choices.feedback: Correct. Her complaint is positional, and a seated set taken while she feels fine cannot reproduce it. Orthostatic measurement is the test that matches the symptom.

choices.text: Document the normal vitals and offer to leave her at home since everything reads fine.
choices.feedback: The numbers look fine in the position where she has no symptoms, which is exactly why they are not reassuring. A single seated set on a patient whose complaint only appears on standing has tested nothing.

choices.text: Check a blood glucose first, since dizziness can be hypoglycemia.
choices.feedback: Reasonable and cheap, and worth doing. But hypoglycemia does not usually switch itself on and off with position. The positional pattern points somewhere else, so do the glucose and still do the orthostatics.

steps.prompt:
Glucose is `106 mg/dL`. After three minutes supine: `HR 84`, `BP 122/72`. You help her stand, stay at her side, and wait one minute.

Standing vitals are below. She says the room is spinning and asks to sit.

Is this test positive?

choices.text: Yes on three separate criteria: systolic dropped 30, diastolic dropped 12, and heart rate rose 32.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Thresholds are a systolic drop of `20` or more, a diastolic drop of `10` or more, or a heart rate rise of `20` or more. She met all three, and her symptoms on standing would have made it positive by themselves.

choices.text: No, because her standing systolic of 92 is still above 90.
choices.feedback: Orthostatic testing measures change, not an absolute threshold. The whole point is that the resting number can look acceptable while the reserve behind it is gone.

choices.text: Yes, but only because she felt dizzy; the numbers themselves are within normal limits.
choices.feedback: The symptom does make it positive on its own, so that instinct is right. But the numbers are not within normal limits here. Every one of the three numeric criteria was crossed as well.

steps.prompt:
Back in the chair she recovers within a minute. You calculate her shock index from the standing set.

What is it, and what does it tell you?

choices.text: 116 divided by 92 equals 1.26, above the 0.9 concern threshold and above 1.0.
choices.feedback: Right. Shock index is heart rate over systolic. Supine she was `84/122`, about `0.69`, which is normal. Standing she is `1.26`. Position alone moved her from normal to a value associated with significant blood loss.

choices.text: 92 divided by 116 equals 0.79, which is borderline but acceptable.
choices.feedback: The formula is inverted. Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure, not the other way around. Flipping it makes a dangerous value look reassuring.

choices.text: It cannot be calculated without knowing her mean arterial pressure.
choices.feedback: Shock index needs only two numbers, heart rate and systolic pressure. `MAP` is a separate and also useful calculation, but it is not an input here.

steps.prompt:
You go back to the history. She says she has been unusually tired for about a week and has been "a little constipated, then some very dark, sticky stools." She takes aspirin daily and started ibuprofen two weeks ago for knee pain.

What do you now think is going on?

choices.text: Dehydration from the furosemide alone, which fully explains the picture.
choices.feedback: Furosemide is a genuine contributor and worth noting. But it does not explain dark sticky stools, and stopping at the easy answer means missing the bleeding underneath it.

choices.text: Slow gastrointestinal bleeding causing hypovolemia, with aspirin and ibuprofen as the likely cause.
choices.feedback: That is the picture. Black, tarry, sticky stool is melena, digested blood from an upper gastrointestinal source. Aspirin plus an anti-inflammatory is a classic combination for gastric bleeding, and a week of slow loss produces exactly this compensated state.

choices.text: An inner ear problem, since the dizziness is clearly positional.
choices.feedback: Positional dizziness does raise inner ear causes, but inner ear vertigo does not drop your blood pressure by 30 points or raise your pulse by 32. The vital signs rule this out.

steps.prompt:
You are ready to move her. She asks to walk to the ambulance because she feels fine sitting down.

What is the right call, and what do you tell the receiving hospital?

choices.text: Let her walk, since she is alert and her seated pressure is acceptable.
choices.feedback: You have direct evidence that standing drops her systolic by 30 and makes her dizzy. Walking her risks a syncopal fall in a patient who is already anemic and on aspirin. The test you just performed is the reason not to.

choices.text: Move her on the stretcher, keep her flat or low, and report the positive orthostatics, the shock index change, and the melena.
choices.feedback: Correct on both halves. She moves without standing, and the report contains the three findings that will drive her workup: positive orthostatics with numbers, a shock index that went from `0.69` to `1.26`, and a week of melena on aspirin and ibuprofen.

choices.text: Move her on the stretcher, but report only that she is dizzy with normal seated vitals.
choices.feedback: The transport decision is right and the report throws away everything you learned. Normal seated vitals is the least informative sentence you could hand over about this patient.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to keep: **when the complaint is positional, the measurement has to be positional too.**

Her seated vitals were unremarkable and would have supported leaving her at home. The orthostatic set turned the same patient into an obvious gastrointestinal bleed with roughly a liter of deficit. Nothing about her changed; only the position she was measured in.

Three numbers did the work. Orthostatic criteria: a systolic drop of `20` or more, a diastolic drop of `10` or more, or a heart rate rise of `20` or more, with symptoms on standing counting by themselves. Shock index: heart rate divided by systolic, moving from `0.69` supine to `1.26` standing. And melena, which is not a vital sign but explained both.

One more thing worth noticing. Her medication list was on the counter the whole time. Aspirin plus ibuprofen in a `74`-year-old is a bleeding risk you can read before you touch the patient, and furosemide means she has less volume reserve to lose. The history was sitting there before any number was taken.

scenarios.title: Triage: 58M, feels weak and off
scenarios.intro:
You are working triage. A `58`-year-old man walks up to the desk with his wife. He says he has felt weak and "off" since yesterday, with some burning when he urinates. No chest pain, no shortness of breath. He drove himself here.

He looks unremarkable. He is polite, oriented, and a little tired. The waiting room is full.

steps.prompt:
You take a triage set. Nothing crosses an obvious alarm line.

What is the right triage thinking here?

choices.text: Note that several values sit at the top of normal together, calculate a shock index, and plan an early recheck.
choices.feedback: Good instinct. `HR 98`, `RR 20` and `37.9 C` are each technically inside normal, but all three sitting at the ceiling at once in a patient with a possible urinary infection is a pattern, not a coincidence. Shock index here is `98/128`, about `0.77`, already borderline.

choices.text: Assign a low acuity since every single value is within normal limits and move on.
choices.feedback: Each number individually supports that, which is exactly how early sepsis gets triaged to the back of the queue. Values clustered at the top of their ranges in a patient with an infection source deserve a second look.

choices.text: Call it a fever and give an antipyretic, then reassess in two hours.
choices.feedback: `37.9 C` is not yet a fever, which is `38.0 C` or higher, and treating the number does nothing about what is producing it. Two hours is also a long interval for a patient whose numbers are all drifting the same way.

steps.prompt:
You put him in a chair in the sub-wait area and recheck at `40` minutes. He says he is "just tired." His wife says he has been answering questions more slowly than usual.

What changed and what does it mean?

choices.text: Every value moved in the same direction, and the wife is reporting a mental status change. This is a deteriorating patient.
choices.feedback: Correct, and the wife's observation is the most important finding in the set. Family noticing that someone is slower than usual is a mental status change reported by the person best positioned to detect it.

choices.text: He now has a real fever, but the blood pressure of 110/64 is still reassuring.
choices.feedback: The fever is real. But `110/64` read in isolation ignores that it was `128/74` forty minutes ago. Falling pressure with a rising pulse is compensation being spent, not stability.

choices.text: The changes are from anxiety and sitting in a busy waiting room.
choices.feedback: Anxiety can raise a pulse and a respiratory rate. It does not raise a temperature by `0.5 C`, drop a systolic by 18, or make a man answer his wife more slowly.

steps.prompt:
Calculate the shock index on both sets: triage was `HR 98`, `BP 128/74`; now `HR 112`, `BP 110/64`.

What is the trend?

choices.text: 0.77 then 1.02, crossing 1.0.
choices.feedback: Right. `98/128` is `0.77` and `112/110` is `1.02`. The heart rate has now passed the systolic. A shock index over `0.9` already signals substantially increased mortality, and over `1.0` it should be treated as shock.

choices.text: 1.31 then 0.98, so he is improving.
choices.feedback: The formula is inverted. Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure. Reversing it turns a deteriorating patient into an improving one, which is the most consequential arithmetic error in this module.

choices.text: 0.77 then 1.02, but that is not meaningful because the blood pressure is still above 90.
choices.feedback: The calculation is right and the conclusion is the trap. Shock index exists precisely because it turns abnormal while both component numbers still look acceptable. Waiting for a systolic under 90 means waiting for decompensation.

steps.prompt:
You bring him back to a room. His skin is warm and flushed rather than cool and clammy. Capillary refill is `3` seconds. A fingerstick glucose reads `148 mg/dL`.

What does warm flushed skin with hypotension tell you?

choices.text: It rules out shock, since shock always produces cold clammy skin.
choices.feedback: That rule applies to hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock, where vessels clamp down. It does not apply here, and treating it as universal is how early septic shock gets missed.

choices.text: It points to distributive shock, where vessels are dilated rather than clamped. With a urinary source and fever, sepsis.
choices.feedback: Exactly. Septic shock is distributive: infection triggers body-wide vasodilation, so the patient runs warm and flushed early and only turns cold and mottled late. The delayed capillary refill tells you perfusion is already suffering despite the warm skin.

choices.text: The glucose of 148 explains the whole presentation.
choices.feedback: A glucose of `148` is mildly elevated and common in acute illness and stress. It explains none of the fever, the falling pressure, the rising pulse or the slowed mentation.

steps.prompt: You give the handoff to the physician. What belongs in it?

choices.text: That he is a 58-year-old with dysuria and a fever of 38.6 C, currently stable.
choices.feedback: Accurate and incomplete in the way that matters. Calling him stable describes the latest snapshot and hides the direction, which is the only thing that separates this patient from the rest of the waiting room.

choices.text: Three timed sets showing every value trending the same way, shock index 0.77 to 1.02 to 1.13, family-reported mental status change, warm flushed skin, capillary refill 3 seconds, urinary source.
choices.feedback: That is the handoff. Timed sets give the trend, the shock index quantifies it, the wife's observation supplies the neurologic finding, and the warm skin names the shock family. The physician can act on that in one sentence.

choices.text: That the automatic cuff readings are unreliable and should be repeated before any decisions are made.
choices.feedback: Confirming a surprising reading manually is good practice, and worth doing. But three consecutive sets all moving the same direction, with matching clinical findings, is not an equipment problem, and treating it as one costs time.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern to keep: **a set of vitals sitting at the ceiling of normal, all at once, in a patient with an infection source, is a trend that has not finished yet.**

The triage set contained no abnormal value. `HR 98` is under `100`. `RR 20` is the top of `12`–`20`. `37.9 C` is under the `38.0 C` fever threshold. Read one at a time, everything passed. Read together, three systems were already responding to something.

Shock index is the tool that made it visible early: `0.77`, then `1.02`, then `1.13`, crossing `1.0` while the systolic was still above `100`. That is the entire argument for the calculation. It turns abnormal before either of its inputs does.

Two other things carried real weight. The wife's report that he was answering more slowly was a mental status change from the person best able to detect it, and family observations of a baseline change should be treated as vital sign data. And the warm, flushed skin with delayed capillary refill named the shock family: distributive, not hypovolemic. If you only know the cold-and-clammy picture, early septic shock does not look like shock at all.
